entries.title: Claiming starfish cousins
entries.body: Star patterns appear on their skin only when friends stack snugly together. The institute suspects they want to claim starfish ancestry, although the creatures themselves are usually asleep. The observation notebook gets a small star whenever this trait appears. Three stars usually mean the assistant laughed far too much that day.

entries.title: A friend's back beats the deep sea
entries.body: Whether in a shallow tank or the deep sea, Tsumi Namako find comfortable gaps. The doctor's records show that their favorite place is a friend's back, regardless of depth. The doctor announced an important discovery, but the assistant asked whether it was merely cute. Their views remain opposed; only the Namako itself stays relaxed.

entries.title: The mostly colorful group
entries.body: Many colors and patterns exist. Unnamed specimens are collectively called the Mostly Colorful Group, a classification unpopular with taxonomists but much loved by their keepers. It does not happen every time, but suddenly returns just as everyone forgets it. Researchers consequently never know when to stop the camera, and the footage grows year after year.

entries.title: A five-direction day
entries.body: Seen from above, their idea of left and right is rather vague. The doctor tested movement in five directions at once; the result was a small wiggle on the spot. The institute tried to repeat the experiment, but matching the conditions only made the subjects less cooperative. Their mood seems to be the greatest enemy of Tsumi Namako research.

entries.title: The secret of stacking ossicles
entries.body: The institute believes tiny stacking ossicles cover their skin. When many creatures pile up, these structures interlock and make the stack surprisingly stable without any effort from its occupants. Children love this habit, but the doctor always adds "probably" to his explanation. The institute oddly insists that research into fictional creatures needs caution too.

entries.title: Another skin-surface meeting
entries.body: No obvious command center has been found. Yet touching two friends makes them decide to stay. The doctor claims decisions are made at skin-surface meetings, though evidence is still lacking. Continued observation suggests it happens more often near friends. Statistics remain elusive: everyone overlaps and becomes impossible to count, leaving the conclusion a little slippery.

entries.title: A calm life without a heart
entries.body: Without a heart-like pump, getting anxious cannot speed up their heartbeat. Even in a crowded tank they look calm, while the observer frets about the final three percent. The doctor tried to invent an impressive scientific name, but nobody could remember its length. The keeper's original phrase, "that nice-looking thing," is now the official name.

entries.title: A migration of millimeters
entries.body: Their tiny tube-like feet rarely move. Upon finding a favorite gap, they suddenly put everything into traveling a few millimeters. The institute calls this a great migration. Diagrams survive in the research notes, but the artist's style makes it impossible to tell a Namako from a loaf of bread. This is a rare document whose words are more reliable than its pictures.

entries.title: A little tentacle check
entries.body: Their mouth tentacles serve as eating hands and tools for poking neighbors. A seemingly motionless stack may actually be gently checking on the friend underneath. Even idly watching the tank reveals tiny changes. A little time-killing soon turns into waiting to see that movement one more time.

entries.title: Even sparkles look delicious
entries.body: Like real sea cucumbers eating seabed sand, they inspect falling sparkles as potential food. Celebration confetti is therefore collected immediately after the festivities. The institute counts the events at the end of each day. Partway through, the discussion becomes a count of cute moments, making the final totals almost useless as research data.

entries.title: The tank's groundskeepers
entries.body: Borrowing the seabed-tilling role of real sea cucumbers, they are called the tank's groundskeepers. Their method is simply rolling into an empty space. Whether this counts as work remains disputed. The doctor's hypothesis is that this is ordinary behavior for the creatures, not a special event. Perhaps only the humans are turning it into a major discovery.

entries.title: Tentacles that forget the collection
entries.body: The doctor says sticky tentacles gather small objects. His diary shows they spend even longer forgetting what they collected, so their reputation for diligence needs another look. A researcher tried using this trait to develop new care methods. The most effective method turned out to be leaving them alone. Sometimes doing nothing is the cutting edge of this research.

entries.title: Slippery hook-and-loop
entries.body: Their slimy tentacles are supposedly a point of pride, nicknamed slippery hook-and-loop. They briefly attach to a friend's back and then separate as if nothing happened. Making a sound during observation can bring everyone to a halt, so the researchers gradually became silent. Only the lab grew strangely quiet: the humans changed more than the Namako.

entries.title: Waiting for visitors from above
entries.body: Inspired by sea cucumbers waiting for marine snow, they look upward with unusual anticipation. What actually falls is usually the next Tsumi Namako. Every record has a small note saying "individual differences apply." Even specimens of the same color differ in temperament, and an exception arrives the moment researchers generalize.

entries.title: Today's preferred sand
entries.body: Even identical sand contains places that feel right and places that feel wrong today. After eighteen days of observation, the doctor approached the distinctly unscientific conclusion: perhaps it is their mood. The doctor plans a special entry for this trait in the card album. It has nothing to do with rarity, but specimens with odd movements are especially popular at the institute.

entries.title: A deep breath from the rear
entries.body: Their real relatives' rear-end water intake is playfully exaggerated into a deep breath from the rear. A startled specimen briefly puffs up, amusing the assistant every time. The subjects seem entirely unaware of being studied. Before and behind the camera, they are equally laid-back. That, at least, is highly reproducible.

entries.title: The napping tree inside
entries.body: Their fictional respiratory tree branches like tiny seaweed. It sways slowly only while they sleep, prompting the doctor to write that even their insides have a napping landscape. On seeing this habit, researchers fetch someone to watch before pressing Record. Important moments consequently go unfilmed, continuing a regrettable institute tradition.

entries.title: Lodger number one was a bubble
entries.body: Stories of fish living inside real sea cucumbers inspired a legend of tiny uninvited lodgers. The only resident found in the tank was a bubble, which the doctor named Lodger Number One. The institute values being fun to watch alongside being useful. Practical scores are low, but the relaxed-slippery score approaches full marks almost every year.

entries.title: Neighbors and fridge raiders
entries.body: An old tale divides their lodgers into quiet residents and greedy eaters. To distinguish them, the institute provisionally calls the groups Neighbors and Fridge Raiders. The doctor's desk holds many notes about this story. The final sheet says "Do not overthink it" in large letters, currently the most faithfully followed research guideline.

entries.title: Slime-resistant housemates
entries.body: Their fictional slime has unusual ingredients, so resident fish are said to resist it. The doctor writes that it must become comfortable with practice, but has no intention of moving inside himself. A hundred small traits together make them seem unexpectedly profound. By the end of an observation session, however, everyone is usually stacked together asleep.

entries.title: Escaping into another stack
entries.body: Usually content to be stacked, a threatened specimen may wriggle and float away. It often lands on another friend, making its escape a rearrangement of the stack. The observation notebook gets a small star whenever this trait appears. Three stars usually mean the assistant laughed far too much that day.

entries.title: A swimming jelly's serious effort
entries.body: Their swimming looks less like graceful motion than a giant jelly desperately remembering an appointment. They take it seriously and stretch proudly for a while after landing. The doctor announced an important discovery, but the assistant asked whether it was merely cute. Their views remain opposed; only the Namako itself stays relaxed.

entries.title: The almost-neckless pudding monster
entries.body: To rival the real deep-sea cucumber's headless chicken monster nickname, the institute invented Almost-Neckless Pudding Monster. Everyone stopped using it the next day because it was too long. It does not happen every time, but suddenly returns just as everyone forgets it. Researchers consequently never know when to stop the camera, and the footage grows year after year.

entries.title: The aquarium ballerina
entries.body: Like real creatures with both monster and dancer nicknames, they are called Slippery Monsters and Aquarium Ballerinas. The same movements suddenly look elegant under a different name. The institute tried to repeat the experiment, but matching the conditions only made the subjects less cooperative. Their mood seems to be the greatest enemy of Tsumi Namako research.

entries.title: Dreaming Tsumi Namako
entries.body: Hearing a story about a scientific name meaning dreamer, the doctor proposed that sleeping specimens dream. Twelve hours watching a motionless stack produced just one finding: they sleep well. Children love this habit, but the doctor always adds "probably" to his explanation. The institute oddly insists that research into fictional creatures needs caution too.

entries.title: Fluttering flaps
entries.body: Swimming specimens have fictional soft, fin-like edges. These flutter like a skirt when they float upward, then flatten on landing as though nothing happened. Continued observation suggests it happens more often near friends. Statistics remain elusive: everyone overlaps and becomes impossible to count, leaving the conclusion a little slippery.

entries.title: After dinner, a friend's back
entries.body: Even swimmers return to the bottom for meals. Some mistake a friend's back for a dining table and stay there, inadvertently contributing to the stack. The doctor tried to invent an impressive scientific name, but nobody could remember its length. The keeper's original phrase, "that nice-looking thing," is now the official name.

entries.title: A walking hourglass
entries.body: In translucent specimens, swallowed sand seems to travel through the body. The doctor calls them walking hourglasses, but their flexible bending makes them useless for telling time. Diagrams survive in the research notes, but the artist's style makes it impossible to tell a Namako from a loaf of bread. This is a rare document whose words are more reliable than its pictures.

entries.title: The sea-pig type
entries.body: Inspired by deep-sea sea pigs, round specimens are called the sea-pig type. They ignore the classification and spend the day finding the softest patch of mud. Even idly watching the tank reveals tiny changes. A little time-killing soon turns into waiting to see that movement one more time.

entries.title: Calmer in the dark?
entries.body: With fictional deep-sea ancestors, they are said to prefer dark tanks. When the lights dimmed, everyone stopped moving. The doctor could not tell calmness from sleep. The institute counts the events at the end of each day. Partway through, the discussion becomes a count of cute moments, making the final totals almost useless as research data.

entries.title: Gourmets of seabed leftovers
entries.body: Seabed leftovers are their delicacy. They inspect sparkles, bubbles and mysterious grains with mouth tentacles, usually taking three seconds to discover something is inedible. The doctor's hypothesis is that this is ordinary behavior for the creatures, not a special event. Perhaps only the humans are turning it into a major discovery.

entries.title: Leaving their insides behind
entries.body: Real sea cucumbers can eject internal organs in defense. This inspired a bold legend of startled specimens leaving their insides behind and fleeing. The game institute keeps it a legend to avoid the cleanup. A researcher tried using this trait to develop new care methods. The most effective method turned out to be leaving them alone. Sometimes doing nothing is the cutting edge of this research.

entries.title: Slippery but persistent
entries.body: Their relatives' regeneration inspired stories of creatures that usually recover after a mishap. The institute's motto, Slippery but Persistent, grew out of this idea. Making a sound during observation can bring everyone to a halt, so the researchers gradually became silent. Only the lab grew strangely quiet: the humans changed more than the Namako.

entries.title: Equipment regrown in fifteen days?
entries.body: Some real species restore gut function in roughly two weeks. The institute wildly embellishes this into a joke about lab equipment regrowing in fifteen days. Equipment does not actually regrow. Every record has a small note saying "individual differences apply." Even specimens of the same color differ in temperament, and an exception arrives the moment researchers generalize.

entries.title: The seventh-day revival
entries.body: Stories of digestive tracts regenerating in about a week inspired a fictional seventh-day revival. On day seven, everyone gives one little wiggle even if nothing has happened. The doctor plans a special entry for this trait in the card album. It has nothing to do with rarity, but specimens with odd movements are especially popular at the institute.

entries.title: A spare workshop inside
entries.body: Drawing on regeneration beginning in the mesentery, the doctor describes an internal spare workshop. Children understand it easily, but researchers always correct him for overstating the case. The subjects seem entirely unaware of being studied. Before and behind the camera, they are equally laid-back. That, at least, is highly reproducible.

entries.title: Too hot to try today
entries.body: Inspired by their relatives' responses to heat and low oxygen, overheated specimens flatten with an expression of Not Today. Cooling restores them, making air conditioning the summer priority. On seeing this habit, researchers fetch someone to watch before pressing Record. Important moments consequently go unfilmed, continuing a regrettable institute tradition.

entries.title: Changing insides, not outfits
entries.body: Hearing that some species seasonally lose internal organs, the doctor named their fictional equivalent Changing Insides. Public relations enjoyed the phrase; the biologists have not officially adopted it. The institute values being fun to watch alongside being useful. Practical scores are low, but the relaxed-slippery score approaches full marks almost every year.

entries.title: Slippery thread launch!
entries.body: Real adhesive defense organs inspired their fictional slippery threads. These cannot defeat an attacker, but are powerful enough to make floor cleaning suddenly difficult. The doctor's desk holds many notes about this story. The final sheet says "Do not overthink it" in large letters, currently the most faithfully followed research guideline.

entries.title: Enough stickiness to leave a sock
entries.body: A slippery thread spreads instantly. The institute measures its stickiness as enough to leave a sock on the floor for a moment. This unit has yet to enter the international system. A hundred small traits together make them seem unexpectedly profound. By the end of an observation session, however, everyone is usually stacked together asleep.

entries.title: Five weeks to refill threads
entries.body: Inspired by regeneration of defensive organs, their fictional slippery-thread supply takes about five weeks to recover. While defenseless, they prefer hiding among friends rather than behind rocks. The observation notebook gets a small star whenever this trait appears. Three stars usually mean the assistant laughed far too much that day.

entries.title: No unnecessary slime
entries.body: Like relatives that do not release all their defenses at once, they consider avoiding unnecessary slime a virtue. Whether this reflects thrift or laziness remains unresolved. The doctor announced an important discovery, but the assistant asked whether it was merely cute. Their views remain opposed; only the Namako itself stays relaxed.

entries.title: The forget-to-launch group
entries.body: Their groups supposedly include thread-launchers, non-launchers and those who forget they intended to launch. The doctor insists that the last group is the largest. It does not happen every time, but suddenly returns just as everyone forgets it. Researchers consequently never know when to stop the camera, and the footage grows year after year.

entries.title: Glowing with happiness
entries.body: Inspired by glowing deep-sea species, they gently glow when happy. At eighty percent tank fill, everyone's glowing wiggle becomes the institute's greatest spectacle. The institute tried to repeat the experiment, but matching the conditions only made the subjects less cooperative. Their mood seems to be the greatest enemy of Tsumi Namako research.

entries.title: Startled sparkles
entries.body: A defense that leaves glowing skin with an enemy inspired their Startled Sparkles move. The startled spot glows for a few seconds while its owner escapes about three centimeters: a modest retreat. Children love this habit, but the doctor always adds "probably" to his explanation. The institute oddly insists that research into fictional creatures needs caution too.

entries.title: New sand patterns every morning
entries.body: Even while stacked, they gradually mix the sand below, like seabed-tilling relatives. By morning the patterns have changed slightly, a difference usually noticed only by the keeper. Continued observation suggests it happens more often near friends. Statistics remain elusive: everyone overlaps and becomes impossible to count, leaving the conclusion a little slippery.

entries.title: The mess-eating crew
entries.body: Their relatives' organic-matter feeding became a fictional talent for eating mess. They will not eat paper scraps, however, so they are almost no help with tidying the lab. The doctor tried to invent an impressive scientific name, but nobody could remember its length. The keeper's original phrase, "that nice-looking thing," is now the official name.

entries.title: The kitchen crew inside
entries.body: Inspired by cooperation with gut microbes, a story gives them a tiny internal kitchen crew. These dependable helpers somehow turn even a mud-only day into a meal. Diagrams survive in the research notes, but the artist's style makes it impossible to tell a Namako from a loaf of bread. This is a rare document whose words are more reliable than its pictures.

entries.title: A potluck inside
entries.body: The doctor explains survival on nutrient-poor mud as an internal potluck. Microbes digest what their host cannot, while borrowing a home inside the creature. Even idly watching the tank reveals tiny changes. A little time-killing soon turns into waiting to see that movement one more time.

entries.title: Fixing the beach's bedhead
entries.body: Their sand-tidying role is called fixing the beach's bedhead. Only the uneven sand along their path becomes a little flatter, leaving the morning tank oddly neat. The institute counts the events at the end of each day. Partway through, the discussion becomes a count of cute moments, making the final totals almost useless as research data.

entries.title: Sand discussing its arrangement
entries.body: An exaggerated account of changes to sand-grain distribution says sand talks and rearranges itself wherever they pass. Nobody has yet recorded these conversations. The doctor's hypothesis is that this is ordinary behavior for the creatures, not a special event. Perhaps only the humans are turning it into a major discovery.

entries.title: The bottom breathes
entries.body: Borrowing their relatives' effects on seabed oxygen, the doctor says a well-populated tank's bottom breathes. It is really the movement of sand, but his phrase is more fun. A researcher tried using this trait to develop new care methods. The most effective method turned out to be leaving them alone. Sometimes doing nothing is the cutting edge of this research.

entries.title: This is artistic work
entries.body: Algae patterns supposedly change only along their paths. Researchers suggest the algae were eaten; the doctor stubbornly records the event as artistic work. Making a sound during observation can bring everyone to a halt, so the researchers gradually became silent. Only the lab grew strangely quiet: the humans changed more than the Namako.

entries.title: The tank's waste-not crew
entries.body: Their role in using aquaculture leftovers became the tank's waste-not job. On spotting scraps, they approach first and consider edibility only after arriving. Every record has a small note saying "individual differences apply." Even specimens of the same color differ in temperament, and an exception arrives the moment researchers generalize.

entries.title: The slippery cycle
entries.body: Research into using oyster-derived organic matter inspired a talent for turning others' leftovers into a fine dinner. The institute calls this the Slippery Cycle rather than an SDG. The doctor plans a special entry for this trait in the card album. It has nothing to do with rarity, but specimens with odd movements are especially popular at the institute.

entries.title: The smaller, the busier
entries.body: Inspired by smaller individuals having higher metabolism per unit weight, the babies are busier than they look. While an adult wiggles once, a baby wiggles three times, falls twice and naps once. The subjects seem entirely unaware of being studied. Before and behind the camera, they are equally laid-back. That, at least, is highly reproducible.

entries.title: Everyone is basically jelly today
entries.body: Like relatives less active in high temperatures, they conserve energy thoroughly on hot days. One research entry simply reads Everyone Is Basically Jelly. The room was thirty-two degrees Celsius. On seeing this habit, researchers fetch someone to watch before pressing Record. Important moments consequently go unfilmed, continuing a regrettable institute tradition.

entries.title: Three minutes of serious effort
entries.body: Real sea cucumbers can crawl surprisingly fast when needed. Their fictional counterparts have three minutes of serious effort, moving ten times faster but then resting just as long. On average, they remain slow. The institute values being fun to watch alongside being useful. Practical scores are low, but the relaxed-slippery score approaches full marks almost every year.

entries.title: Rather stack than swim
entries.body: Inspired by the many non-swimming species, some prefer being stacked to swimming. Even a current cannot shift them; only their neighbor wobbles in mild annoyance. The doctor's desk holds many notes about this story. The final sheet says "Do not overthink it" in large letters, currently the most faithfully followed research guideline.

entries.title: Swimmers are a little proud
entries.body: Real swimming species inspired a world where swimmers show off a little. They return to a pile of friends halfway through the performance, so the audience regards it as a landing trick. A hundred small traits together make them seem unexpectedly profound. By the end of an observation session, however, everyone is usually stacked together asleep.

entries.title: Colorful regional types
entries.body: The diversity of harvested sea cucumbers inspired many fictional regional types. Their patterns, slime and nap durations differ, with particularly extreme regional differences in napping. The observation notebook gets a small star whenever this trait appears. Three stars usually mean the assistant laughed far too much that day.

entries.title: The slippery exchange fair
entries.body: Historical sea-cucumber trade inspired a fictional Slippery Exchange Fair. Instead of buying or selling, participants show off their patterns and finish stacked in one shared pile. The doctor announced an important discovery, but the assistant asked whether it was merely cute. Their views remain opposed; only the Namako itself stays relaxed.

entries.title: Scientifically worrying labels
entries.body: Like fisheries handling many species, the institute's shelves bear over twenty kinds of labels. Thirty percent say things such as Probably Blue or Very Round: scientifically worrying names. It does not happen every time, but suddenly returns just as everyone forgets it. Researchers consequently never know when to stop the camera, and the footage grows year after year.

entries.title: Indistinguishable while sleeping
entries.body: Inspired by dried relatives becoming hard to identify, sleeping specimens shrink and become difficult to distinguish. The doctor gave everyone a name tag; by morning only the tags were neatly stacked. The institute tried to repeat the experiment, but matching the conditions only made the subjects less cooperative. Their mood seems to be the greatest enemy of Tsumi Namako research.

entries.title: The elusive Becha de Tsumi
entries.body: The dried product beche-de-mer inspired an imaginary dish called Becha de Tsumi. Only its name exists. Nobody knows the recipe, so it can never join the menu. Children love this habit, but the doctor always adds "probably" to his explanation. The institute oddly insists that research into fictional creatures needs caution too.

entries.title: Popular colors hide best
entries.body: Reversing the history of valuable species disappearing first, popular colors in this world hide best. Finding a rare specimen is exciting, but it is usually tucked beneath its friends. Continued observation suggests it happens more often near friends. Statistics remain elusive: everyone overlaps and becomes impossible to count, leaving the conclusion a little slippery.

entries.title: Pretending not to be found
entries.body: Rather than flee, they prefer pretending not to be found. They stay still beside transparent glass, fully visible to researchers but looking pleased with their successful concealment. The doctor tried to invent an impressive scientific name, but nobody could remember its length. The keeper's original phrase, "that nice-looking thing," is now the official name.

entries.title: One newcomer is a major event
entries.body: Inspired by resources that recover slowly, they make not multiplying in a hurry a way of life. A single newcomer triggers a magnificent fanfare. Another friend is a major event. Diagrams survive in the research notes, but the artist's style makes it impossible to tell a Namako from a loaf of bread. This is a rare document whose words are more reliable than its pictures.

entries.title: Hand stackers and automatic stackers
entries.body: The diversity of small and industrial fisheries inspired hand-stacking and automatic-stacking artisans. In the end, the neatest stack usually happens by accident. Even idly watching the tank reveals tiny changes. A little time-killing soon turns into waiting to see that movement one more time.

entries.title: Friends from faraway seas
entries.body: Historical journeys to Asian markets inspired stories of distant companions meeting in a tank. Despite different colors and patterns, touching two others makes them friends immediately. The institute counts the events at the end of each day. Partway through, the discussion becomes a count of cute moments, making the final totals almost useless as research data.

entries.title: Northern types love cold packs
entries.body: Commercial species in cold seas inspired northern types. Their slime is slightly firmer and cold water improves their mood. In warm rooms, they stay close to the cold packs. The doctor's hypothesis is that this is ordinary behavior for the creatures, not a special event. Perhaps only the humans are turning it into a major discovery.

entries.title: Slippery almost everywhere
entries.body: Drawing on their relatives' range from polar to tropical waters, they are slippery almost everywhere. Their personal preferences are still precise: they are extremely fussy about the right temperature. A researcher tried using this trait to develop new care methods. The most effective method turned out to be leaving them alone. Sometimes doing nothing is the cutting edge of this research.

entries.title: The ancient stacking delivery
entries.body: Eighth-century records of sea cucumbers traveling from Noto to the capital inspired an ancient stacking delivery story. Its fictional wooden label says Six kin, provided they are stacked three high along the way. Making a sound during observation can bring everyone to a halt, so the researchers gradually became silent. Only the lab grew strangely quiet: the humans changed more than the Namako.

entries.title: Imperial stacking etiquette?
entries.body: Expanding on Noto sea cucumbers appearing in the Engishiki, the doctor jokes that the imperial court had Tsumi Namako stacking etiquette. Naturally, the historical text says nothing of the sort. Every record has a small note saying "individual differences apply." Even specimens of the same color differ in temperament, and an exception arrives the moment researchers generalize.

entries.title: Winter curls in the corner
entries.body: Noto's winter food traditions inspired specimens curling up in a tank corner during winter. They supposedly enjoy seeing snow, but the lab's tiny window has prevented confirmation. The doctor plans a special entry for this trait in the card album. It has nothing to do with rarity, but specimens with odd movements are especially popular at the institute.

entries.title: A slippery route across the sea
entries.body: Northern Australia's trepang trade inspired an old tale of a slippery route across the sea. The usual telling has them traveling stacked in cargo boxes rather than sitting aboard a ship. The subjects seem entirely unaware of being studied. Before and behind the camera, they are equally laid-back. That, at least, is highly reproducible.

entries.title: Touch two and become friends
entries.body: Pre-colonial overseas exchanges inspired creatures greeting one another with slime before words. According to the doctor, first-meeting etiquette needs only one rule: touch two and become friends. On seeing this habit, researchers fetch someone to watch before pressing Record. Important moments consequently go unfilmed, continuing a regrettable institute tradition.

entries.title: A whole dictionary of local names
entries.body: Trade's traces in language inspired different names along every coast. The institute calls them Tsumi Namako, but their local names supposedly fill an entire dictionary. The institute values being fun to watch alongside being useful. Practical scores are low, but the relaxed-slippery score approaches full marks almost every year.

entries.title: Shrinking during naps
entries.body: Drawing on the changes caused by drying, they shrink dramatically during naps. Waking restores their length, but the stretch takes a few seconds, leaving them briefly with oddly short faces. The doctor's desk holds many notes about this story. The final sheet says "Do not overthink it" in large letters, currently the most faithfully followed research guideline.

entries.title: Tiny doughnuts under the microscope
entries.body: Like identification by microscopic ossicles, the doctor classifies stacking ossicles under a microscope. Shapes include stars, wheels and a type that looks unmistakably like tiny doughnuts. A hundred small traits together make them seem unexpectedly profound. By the end of an observation session, however, everyone is usually stacked together asleep.

entries.title: Color personality tests: no evidence
entries.body: Different species' traits inspired slightly different personalities by color. Red is impatient, blue sleepy and yellow prone to falling. There is absolutely no statistical evidence. The observation notebook gets a small star whenever this trait appears. Three stars usually mean the assistant laughed far too much that day.

entries.title: Cards reunite distant friends
entries.body: Links between small fishing villages and distant markets inspired friends reuniting through cards. As the collection grows, the tank's chart of companions grows more lively too. The doctor announced an important discovery, but the assistant asked whether it was merely cute. Their views remain opposed; only the Namako itself stays relaxed.

entries.title: Even SSR deserves a gentle look
entries.body: Taking high prices and overharvesting as a cautionary example, the institute gently observes its rarest specimens. An SSR draw gives the doctor three seconds of joy before he quietly returns to the album. It does not happen every time, but suddenly returns just as everyone forgets it. Researchers consequently never know when to stop the camera, and the footage grows year after year.

entries.title: More than cute
entries.body: Their relatives' ecological work inspired cute but industrious tank-tidying creatures. They are unaware of doing any work and simply eat and sleep. The institute tried to repeat the experiment, but matching the conditions only made the subjects less cooperative. Their mood seems to be the greatest enemy of Tsumi Namako research.

entries.title: The slippery civil-engineering team
entries.body: Their seabed-working role earned them the Slippery Civil-Engineering Team title. They swallow sand, release it somewhere else and nap on it. The department head does exactly the same job. Children love this habit, but the doctor always adds "probably" to his explanation. The institute oddly insists that research into fictional creatures needs caution too.

entries.title: Being stacked is the easiest job
entries.body: Their job changes with location: shallow-water cleaners, deep-water collectors of falling material, and tank occupants whose main duty is being stacked. The last job suddenly becomes much easier. Continued observation suggests it happens more often near friends. Statistics remain elusive: everyone overlaps and becomes impossible to count, leaving the conclusion a little slippery.

entries.title: Strange behavior when the camera arrives
entries.body: Deep-sea discoveries inspired a lab superstition that placing a camera triggers new strange behavior. The latest observation had everyone leaning in the same direction for three seconds. The doctor tried to invent an impressive scientific name, but nobody could remember its length. The keeper's original phrase, "that nice-looking thing," is now the official name.

entries.title: Too transparent for the card photo
entries.body: Transparent specimens are both a researcher's delight and a headache. Their meals are plainly visible inside, but in card photographs they blend into the background and are usually lost. Diagrams survive in the research notes, but the artist's style makes it impossible to tell a Namako from a loaf of bread. This is a rare document whose words are more reliable than its pictures.

entries.title: A secret recipe too wet to read
entries.body: Research into nourishment from poor mud inspired a secret recipe for turning mud into a fine meal. A recipe book exists, but every page is too wet to read. Even idly watching the tank reveals tiny changes. A little time-killing soon turns into waiting to see that movement one more time.

entries.title: Stacking mode
entries.body: Their relatives' adjustable body-wall stiffness inspired Soft Mode and Stacking Mode. They firm up slightly only on touching two friends, which underlies the game's rule for staying in place. The institute counts the events at the end of each day. Partway through, the discussion becomes a count of cute moments, making the final totals almost useless as research data.

entries.title: Good posture only for group photos
entries.body: They become floppy while sleeping and straighten slightly for commemorative photos. The doctor insists they know about the camera, although coincidence is more likely. The doctor's hypothesis is that this is ordinary behavior for the creatures, not a special event. Perhaps only the humans are turning it into a major discovery.

entries.title: The tank's health inspectors
entries.body: Research on improving bottom sediment inspired a tank health-inspector job. They gather over dirty sand, so the doctor checks their queue before reaching for instruments. A researcher tried using this trait to develop new care methods. The most effective method turned out to be leaving them alone. Sometimes doing nothing is the cutting edge of this research.

entries.title: Someone's leftovers, another's feast
entries.body: Inspired by integrated aquaculture, their motto is Someone's Leftovers Are Another's Feast. Scraps, algae and organic matter in sand pass around a small slippery cycle within the tank. Making a sound during observation can bring everyone to a halt, so the researchers gradually became silent. Only the lab grew strangely quiet: the humans changed more than the Namako.

entries.title: Nobody can count the babies
entries.body: Long-running sea-cucumber aquaculture research inspired a nursery team. Its most important task is counting babies, but they overlap halfway through and the count is lost every time. Every record has a small note saying "individual differences apply." Even specimens of the same color differ in temperament, and an exception arrives the moment researchers generalize.

entries.title: Official summer sluggishness
entries.body: Inspired by reduced warm-season activity, they have official summer sluggishness. Nobody wiggles on hot days, so only the celebration effects dance energetically while the creatures become ornaments. The doctor plans a special entry for this trait in the card album. It has nothing to do with rarity, but specimens with odd movements are especially popular at the institute.

entries.title: The eraser incident
entries.body: Human rubbish reaching the deep sea inspired lessons that not everything falling from above is food. The cautionary tale is the day they surrounded the doctor's dropped eraser. The subjects seem entirely unaware of being studied. Before and behind the camera, they are equally laid-back. That, at least, is highly reproducible.

entries.title: A fanfare for every new friend
entries.body: Reflecting real local losses from overharvesting, their stories treat losing companions as a major event. Every new friend therefore gets a fanfare. Extravagant celebration is this world's custom. On seeing this habit, researchers fetch someone to watch before pressing Record. Important moments consequently go unfilmed, continuing a regrettable institute tradition.

entries.title: A slippery three-way dilemma
entries.body: Sustainable fishery management inspired the dilemma: do not increase them too much, do not reduce them too much, but still collect cards. The doctor calls it the Slippery Three-Way Dilemma. The institute values being fun to watch alongside being useful. Practical scores are low, but the relaxed-slippery score approaches full marks almost every year.

entries.title: The town's watchful Namako
entries.body: Inspired by resources supporting coastal communities, each town supposedly has a watchful Namako. It does nothing special, simply resting in a stack in the square. That alone feels reassuring. The doctor's desk holds many notes about this story. The final sheet says "Do not overthink it" in large letters, currently the most faithfully followed research guideline.

entries.title: Research has only just begun
entries.body: Borrowing a little of every strange real trait, they eat mud, breathe through their rear, sometimes swim, glow when startled and relax on touching two friends. The doctor says research has only just begun. A hundred small traits together make them seem unexpectedly profound. By the end of an observation session, however, everyone is usually stacked together asleep.
